en: At that time, when the Dharma for the Holy Immovable Honored One to pacify and stabilize the state and the nation was being taught, Vairocana Tathāgata,

out of compassion for all sentient beings who were constantly wandering through birth and death within the ocean of afflictions and suffering, unable to emerge from the triple world and enduring manifold miseries, [spoke as follows].
Therefore, they continue to create immeasurable karmic actions of suffering in succession without interruption.
For the sake of delivering all sentient beings from this, I [act].
Within the three realms, he manifests a body of sovereign majesty and radiant light,
known as the Vidyārāja Acala-vajra;
he is able to bestow peace, happiness, and benefit upon gods and humans.
It will bring peace and stability to the state and the family,
ensuring no decline or calamity. Should there be lands beset by many disasters,
such as the sun and moon losing their courses or malevolent stars manifesting strange portents, [this shall pacify them].
They oppress one another, floods and droughts are out of season,
and because sentient beings have meager merit, the devas and nāgas abandon them;
when such a time is encountered—
Inauspicious omens arise in competition with one another without ceasing; grain becomes expensive, leading to hunger and cold; ghosts and demons spread their influence;
pestilence, malevolent spirits, tigers, and wolves cause havoc;
violent winds, frost, hail, and venomous insects and locusts swarm.
Enemies frequently arise and the multitude of rulers turn their backs on the state;
there are many bandits and thieves, and wars are repeatedly instigated.
Calamities occur in succession without end.
The benevolent king of that land,
if he knows there is such a person who holds the vidyā-mantra,
should establish a mind of great compassion toward them.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings within the realm,
he practices the secret dharma of the majestic power of the Great Vidyārāja,
causing all sentient beings to increase in merit and virtue.
Giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse, he abandoned all karmic actions that lead to suffering.
At that time, the king conceived a great spirit of faith and joy,
as well as a mind of firm resolve, and summoned such a great vidyādhara.
One should relinquish wealth, silks, clothing, rare curiosities, gardens, groves, houses, elephants, horses,
carriages, slaves, servants, and all manner of other excellent and auspicious objects, and address them as follows:
"For the sake of all sentient beings and because the land is in turmoil, you,
O Venerable One, should bring this dharma to fulfillment for me.
I have heard that the power of this dharma is inconceivable."
"For you, for me, and for all sentient beings, you should quickly establish this sublime Dharma to eliminate all calamities and misfortunes.
Whatever you require, you may take as you wish; I shall never go against your will."
At that time, having received this request, the vidyādhara shall not give rise to weariness or aversion,
but shall practice and venerate according to the instructions.
One must purely fashion an image of the Vidyārāja Acala,
as well as the celestial kings of the eight directions along with their retinues,
constructing them according to the Dharma in accordance with one's own capacity.
It may be made of gold, silver, or even copper, iron, clay, or wood, or painted;
it should be eight finger-widths in height,
with both arms and the body bearing the marks of a youth.
His body is massive and full, his complexion like gold;
his hair hangs down to the left, and his majestic countenance is extremely wrathful.
He holds a sword of wisdom in his right hand and grasps a noose in his left.
He sits upon a golden lotus stone, his radiance blazing intensely;
many of these flames take the form of garuḍas.
This image is enshrined within the royal palace.
Furthermore, in the central portion of all the palaces, residences,
and dwellings occupied by the hundred officials and the common people, one should install this image.
At the eight directional sites of protection, one should instead fashion the four-armed Great Vajra Wrathful Body.
Deep blue-black in color, he is massive, full, and majestic.
His eyes and mouth are wide open, with sharp fangs protruding upward.
He holds a sword in his right hand and a lasso in his left.
His two upper arms, positioned on either side of his mouth, form the wrathful mudrā.
His body stands upon an eight-spoked vajra wheel,
which encloses him within.
On the outside, he manifests eight three-pronged vajra-wheels at his head,
which further possess garuḍa-flames;
he sits atop Mount Sumeru made of the four great jewels.
As well as the eight classes of devas and their retinues;
furthermore, there are the original patterns for casting the golden wheel.
From the royal palace above down to the common people below, all shall practice this method.
It is impossible that they would not act universally;
you should all install images in your dwellings and harbor no fear.
From the beginning, my original vow has been never to abandon sentient beings.
Always dwelling in one place, he thoroughly purifies all that is defiled and turbid.
He offers the remains of food as an act of worship and receives the five-syllable heart-mantra of the Tathāgata Vairocana.

Furthermore, for sentient beings in military service, one should also provide this *Sarva-mantra* and the remains of the food offering (*ucchista-bali*) to cause their merit to increase and become superior.
Within the royal palace, one should perform offerings according to the ritual on the first and fifteenth days of every month.
With various fragrant flowers, exquisite banners, precious nets, ghee lamps,
*argha* water, precious vases, precious vessels, sublime unguents,
delicacies of superior flavor, rare and wonderful foods, and various medicinal decoctions.
He also presented various kinds of sublime music.
At that time, the king abandoned his prideful mind and developed a humble heart;
he personally offered prayers for the sake of the entire realm and all its people.
Reverently making offerings, circumambulating, and prostrating,
they earnestly entreated [the deity] and made sublime vows.
Their power of merit increased, and the people lived in peace and happiness, free from all calamities.
Every spring and autumn, one should perform offerings according to the Dharma in accordance with the households of the teachings,
manifesting the king’s profound sincerity and never becoming weary toward all sentient beings.
To seek supreme merit for the borders of our nation,
after these eight ritual sites have been thus arranged,
all calamities and misfortunes shall be forever severed within that land.
The devas and nāgas rejoice and take pity upon sentient beings;
the Buddhas shall always protect and mind all living beings.
For the sake of empowerment, may we all cultivate shame and remorse and practice the ten wholesome paths together.
The national borders will naturally become peaceful, stable, and abundant;
its people shall enjoy every form of happiness.
Under the transformation of this benevolent king, their merit and virtue will increase manifold, succeeding one another without end.
His lifespan increased and his kingdom flourished;
possessing great majesty like that of a lion king, none could overcome him.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him in verse:
I, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, pacify and stabilize the state and the nation;
manifesting the majesty and sovereign power of the Dharma, I am known as Acala Vidyārāja,
who severs the karma of the three evil paths for all sentient beings.
Able to leave behind all eight difficulties, so that those within the three realms may attain peace;
thus I praise and explain the practice, as well as the ritual procedures for the door,
the offerings, the appropriate times, and the conjunctions of the lunar mansions, days, and planets.
Each and every one is empowered; Pure and free from defilement, they abide in the contemplative practice of the three secrets. Whatever they do is endowed with dignified deportment;
Rising before noon on the third day, They achieve completion after noon on the fifth day.
After midnight, seal the rear gate; with the Great Sun firmly established, the Great Compassionate One’s Root Name—the five-syllable Heart Mantra King—was commanded to circulate everywhere.
Let the military hosts all receive and wear it.
Establish the honored image, with mudrās clearly and distinctly formed;
the youthful body is majestic and wrathful, its facial features fully perfected.
The ritual procedures and offerings are all in accord with the instructions.
The general maṇḍala and the fundamental self-differentiation follow the sequence of methods as described above;
for each pacification, one should begin before the painted image,
starting from Kauśika and proceeding clockwise to Īśāna.
Within a perimeter of one hundred yojanas, the Greatly Wrathful One with four arms has a single topknot hanging down to the left; his body is deep blue-black in color,
and he sits in the half-lotus posture atop Mount Meru, having accomplished the *khadga* (sword).
Fierce flames arise from the heart, appearing like golden-winged garuḍas.
The eight devas abide in their original positions, facing the Honored One before them;
holding their respective mudrās and reciting their mantras, they all present offerings to the retinue.
The dragon deities all rejoice, extolling and praising the king of men.
The eight difficulties cannot invade him; all share in peace and happiness.
Those who were difficult to subdue, their calamities and transformations are naturally eliminated.
Even if one should sever the life-force of another within the midst of a military array,
by virtue of wearing this mantra, the Great Being’s power will provide empowerment such that the causes of enmity and harm are forever severed, and one shall be born in the supreme Akṣobhya realm.
That king resides nearby; his two arms are his fundamental body, which is yellow in color.
He sits upon a golden mountain, manifesting the form of Kumāra, adorned with banners, flowers, and canopies, and arrayed with various exquisite ornaments.
On the morning of the fifteenth day of the first month,
the King personally gazed upon the remains of the food he had renounced; he offered them to Acala,
making this offering without giving rise to doubt, thereby attaining the flavor of true reality.
I dedicate this to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
may my vows fulfill the sentient beings within the great trichiliocosm, so that all may dwell together in peace and happiness.
Next, the method for the ritual of pacifying and stabilizing according to the occasion is explained.
When one wishes to perform the rite of pacification (śāntika), one first begins in the east;
in the east, one selects an excellent and superior site.
Free from all impurities and evils, this site is empowered by the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*).
At the location where the ritual stake is to be planted, one should dig a pit three cubits deep and three cubits wide,
and smear it with cow dung (*gomaya*).
Prepare scented ointments, argha water, lamps, food offerings, ghee, milk, and cakes.
Construct a separate square maṇḍala measuring one cubit,
and place an image of the principal deity upon this altar.
Adorned with banners and flowers, one should extensively arrange offerings.
At midnight, one should perform the *karmapatha* of the door.
The place where one dwells should be spread with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, pearls, amber, and the seven precious jewels upon the wheel.
Within the center of the wheel, drive a blade of tempered iron into the ground while reciting the mantra one thousand and eighty times;
strike it once for each recitation until the count is complete.
Then, scatter the five grains at the four corners.
The ground was immediately filled level with earth.
When it was time to perform the consecration,
they waited from the afternoon until before midnight for an auspicious moment.
Immediately thereafter, he subdued Houye Huoma.
On the four sides of the altar,
they followed the colors of the five directions.
Stabilize it with silk, brocade, coins, and cloth.
Once the merit has been completed during the phase of the rising dawn,
place upon that stabilized site a plain image of the Four-Armed Acala Vidyārāja.
Together with their respective original celestial retinues,
each holding their own mudrās, incense, and flowers, they offered worship toward the Honored One.
As for the white image, it should be made according to the height and proportions of the body of a *rāja*.
Before his work was finished,
he opened his eyes and made vast offerings, providing great music.
Having caused all these excellent [deities] to be stationed according to this,
one should likewise pervade the eight directions,
as described above.
He then installed the two-armed root Acala Vidyārāja within the royal palace,
establishing him according to the ritual and arranging him as prescribed by the teachings.
He subsequently issued commands to the kings and officials throughout the four directions.
From the high ministers and hundred officials down to the common people, within their respective dwellings,
they should establish the Immovable Image as previously described and recite the Five-Syllable Heart Mantra while walking.
One should issue strict decrees to further exhort and admonish [the people],
ensuring that the offering of leftover food (*ucchista-bhoga*) is never interrupted.
Together, let us uphold the boundaries of the realm so that peace and stability prevail everywhere.
Even if someone were to sing, dance, play, laugh, or give rise to a mind of contempt before this Great Holy Honored One,
this Great Vidyārāja would not feel revulsion or weariness.
I bestow supreme merit.
If any sentient beings offer me even a small portion of leftover food as an offering,
it is equivalent to offering immeasurable, exquisite, and wonderful treasures from the ten directions.
Food and drink of a hundred flavors, clothing and bedding,
the most excellent medicinal decoctions, palaces made of the seven treasures,
elephants, horses, carriages, and servants.
The merit of this offering is no different from that [of the former],
yet it exceeds it by hundreds of thousands of millions of times;
it thus constitutes a truly vast and sublime offering.
Regarding that which is most appropriate when performing the offerings:
red-colored garments are supremely auspicious.
Next, the construction of the *hu-mo* hearth and the implements to be used will be explained.
When performing the *humā* rite,
one should fashion a *humā* hearth before the Vidyārāja, one cubit wide and half a cubit deep.
One should take earth from the four sides of the city or town where the ritual is performed, along with earth from the banks of flowing water and rivers.
Then, having empowered various fragrances and mixed them with clay,
one uses this to plaster the hearth-altar (kuṇḍa-maṇḍala),
and further smears it with cow dung (gomaya).
At the center is the sword mudrā.
To the left of the practitioner is the position of the King,
followed by the position of the Minister.
Next is the rank of Great General,
followed by the rank of Lord of the Earth;
one must personally enter the maṇḍala and give rise to a heart of utmost sincerity.
Within the inner sanctum of the central position of the site, no more than three persons may be present.
Outside the altar, at a distance of seven paces from each of the four sides,
they shall stand in strict formation, donning armor and holding weapons exactly according to the ritual law.
Furthermore, they performed various kinds of sublime music and presented extensive offerings,
widely proclaiming the King’s command before the Great Holy Honored One for the sake of all sentient beings.
One should properly install the deity of the original direction along with its retinue according to the Dharma.
When cultivating merit, one shall see signs of fire;
should any inauspicious omens arise, they should be warded off in accordance with the instructions.
Once it has been securely installed,
summon three persons capable of spiritual practice at that very spot and have them maintain the rite,
burning incense, sweeping, and making offerings at the three times of day.
On the first and fifteenth days of every month,
one should offer lamps, food and drink, and various kinds of music according to the Dharma;
thus the devas will rejoice and protect this realm.
There shall be no decline or misfortune;
all will be peaceful and happy.
When opening the door, use four *liang* or two *liang* of cow ghee.
The five grains, *kṛṣṇatila* (black sesame), milk, curd, food and drink,
fruit, cakes, wax candles,
mung beans, unguents, the five flavors, aloeswood, sandalwood, and *sugandhaka*.
Camphor, saffron, guggulu, human breast-milk, white mustard seeds, and honey;
[the ritual] follows the age of the patron.
The sacrificial wood (samidh) shall be twelve finger-widths long.
Mung beans, white glue, and *bhr̥ṅgarāja* are used as substitutes for the royal garments to represent [the deity] in the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*).
This is no different from making offerings and gazing upon [the deity] in person.
For each sub-prefecture, there shall be one forged iron stake and one copper wheel; each stake shall be eight finger-widths in length,
with more than half of it being single-pronged and possessing sharp edges.
The shape of the pegs below should be flush with the rim of the wheel.
The wheel is four finger-widths wide and one cubit in diameter.
Within it are eight spokes, and on the outside, at each of the eight directions, there emerges the head of a three-pronged half-vajra.
The wheel-rim has a hole large enough to accommodate a wedge of tempered steel;
there are two golden-bronze *huma* ladles;
and for each settlement, one banner of Achala (Acala).
This is one standard of the Heavenly King;
when the army and cavalry are on the march,
it shall immediately be carried at the front.
The Great General follows behind.
If it is not being carried out,
install it at its original location and ensure it is not defiled.
When performing the homa,
whether at the beginning or the end, one should offer three ladles of ghee and carefully observe its signs.
If the land and its people suffer from calamities,
transformations, or inauspicious signs resulting from good or evil deeds,
one should expel them according to the teachings.
If there are such evil signs, and one does not perform meritorious deeds,
there will surely be a manifestation of retribution within three years.
Otherwise, perform a separate great merit-making rite;
wherever one turns [the merit] for assistance, it must be done.
When performing the *humpha* ritual:
The characteristics of fire are a clockwise spiral with flames rising straight upward;
or it may produce the wondrous sounds of musical instruments such as bells and gongs,
or take the form of an image— these are signs of great auspiciousness.
Furthermore, if one performs inauspicious rites on the left side,
creating the forms of birds and beasts and making the sound "ha ha," there will likewise be calamities in that land.
When sentient beings suffer from hunger and cold, or when floods, droughts, and untimely weather cause the people to die of starvation,
one should perform the rite for pacifying calamities to dispel them.
This is especially appropriate during the *humā* period.
If smoke and mist arise from the fire and hang down in darkness,
and the fire in the hearth is extinguished such that the offering is not accomplished,
there will also be secret signs of treachery and harm upon that ground.
One should employ the methods of subjugation to repel them.
Regarding the four types of signs of good and evil mentioned above,
one must apply the utmost care to examine them minutely and repel them according to their specific characteristics.
If performing a rite for pacification (śāntika), one should use wood from milky trees;
the mudrā in the hearth is that of the wheel;
and the mantra syllables, food, clothing, and garments should be white.
If performing the rite of increase (*puṣṭi*), use wood from a white altar;
the ritual implement in the hearth is the banner seal (*dhvajamudrā*);
and both food and clothing are red.
If one wishes to perform the rite of attraction (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one should cast lotuses into the fire;
if no other flowers are available, they may serve as a substitute.
This is the lotus mudrā within the hearth.
Both clothing and food are red.
When performing subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one should cast in wood from the *kaṭuka* tree, thorns, *kārpāsa* pods, poisonous substances, and so forth;
both clothing and food are black.
If a Golden Wheel-turning King acts as a stabilizing ruler for the sentient beings of the four continents,
he may stabilize them within a circumference of ten thousand yojanas;
if a Silver Wheel-turning King, he may stabilize them within eight thousand yojanas.
If it is a copper-wheel-turning king, he pacifies within sixty yojanas;
if it is an iron-wheel-turning king, he pacifies within three thousand yojanas;
for the sake of the sentient beings of his own realm, he pacifies within a hundred yojanas.
Within each of the four directions of the royal city for a distance of one thousand *li*,
the King shall establish a pacifying station at a convenient location beyond one hundred *li*,
provided that it does not exceed its designated boundary.
Thus it is accomplished.
The rituals for pacification and stabilization, as well as the maṇḍala and its images,
and all the materials required, have now been briefly explained.
You sentient beings, having generated the bodhicitta for the sake of all sentient beings,
should practice according to the instructions by constructing the *humā* hearth and arranging the images.
When performing the act of subduing, one should not do so openly by name;
it must be done in secret so that those in the vicinity do not know.
Only the supervisor knows this.
Medicines must first be prepared and kept ready;
whatever is essential for one's own journey should be used immediately.
This secret dharma is not permitted for those who have left the household life to practice.
Those who uphold this dharma must personally prostrate to the various devas during all offerings they perform.
Because those who have left the household life possess the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts,
they cause others to feel uneasy and dare not receive their prostrations;
consequently, whatever blessings or merit they seek will not be accomplished.
Those who violate this shall commit a grave offense.
For this reason, it was not transmitted to those who have left the household life.
This original method belongs to the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi.
This was received from the Great Master of India;
do not transmit it to others.
It is permitted to be bestowed only upon laypeople.
The practitioner must keep this secret, most secret.
In the Western Regions, this dharma is held in profound esteem;
even when one wishes to practice it secretly, one does not allow other countries to know of its existence.
For this reason, in the Western lands, the succession of the lineage has been maintained without interruption.
Furthermore, in the West, those who are stingy with the Dharma merely transmit the venerable forms;
among all the schools, these are regarded as the great protection.
Little do they realize that there are methods for pacifying and stabilizing the state and the family.
The Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi transmitted this ritual manual to the King, Wang Guang.

It contains the methods for the banners and flags of the Eight Directional Heavenly Kings of Acala, who crushes enemy forces, as well as the mantra for the Descent of the Enemies of the Eight Directions. For the eastern direction, one should make a white banner.
On the banner is depicted the Heavenly King Śakra,
holding a single-pronged vajra in his right hand and resting his left hand upon his hip.
Riding upon a six-tusked white elephant,
a person holding a white banner recites the mantra for Śakra Devendra’s subjugation of enemies.
The spell says:
Oṃ indrayāṇi vabhūpate hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. When proceeding toward the east:
First, raise this banner.
Visualize Śakra, Lord of the Devas, leading an immeasurable host of celestial attendants,
brandishing various weapons to charge against that host of enemies.
In the southeast, one should place a yellow flag.
Upon the flag is painted the four-armed Agni (Fire God),
riding a blue sheep, with flames emanating from his entire body.
The right hand performs the gesture of granting fearlessness;
the second holds a rosary;
the left hand holds a staff of the sages (khaṭvāṅga).
Second, one holds a water jar.
The person holding the banner recites the mantra for the subjugation of enemies by the Fire Deity (Agnideva).
The vidyā is as follows:
Oṃ āgneye arthāptaye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. When traveling toward the southeast.
First, raise this banner.
Visualize the Fire Deity leading an immeasurable army of fire-spirits (*agni-rākṣasa*), brandishing various weapons, charging against the host of enemies.
In the south, fashion a black banner.
On the banner is depicted the deity Yama,
riding a water buffalo and holding the banner of Yama in his right hand.
With his left hand resting on his hip,
the flag-bearer recites the mantra for subduing enemies by King Yama.
The vidyā is as follows:
Oṃ yamāntakṛtpadaprade hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [When walking southward:]
First, raise this banner and visualize King Yama leading an immeasurable army of spirits,
brandishing various weapons to charge against that host of enemies.
In the southwest, one should place a banner of a wrathful color;
upon the banner is painted the Lord of Rākṣasas,
riding a lion.
His right hand holds a sword;
his left hand rests on his hip.
A standard-bearer recites the Rākṣasa-lord's "Subduing Enemies" mantra.
The mantra is: Oṃ tīrthikṣāsa-dhiphate hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. When traveling toward the southwest, [recite this].
First, hoist this banner.
Visualize the Rākṣasa Lord leading immeasurable rākṣasas,
brandishing various weapons, charging into the enemy host.
In the western direction, one should make a red flag.
On the flag, one should paint Varuṇa,
riding upon a tortoise.
In his right hand he holds a snake-noose;
his left hand rests across his waist.
Upon the head of this deity are seven dragon heads, shaped like serpents.
The flag-bearer recites the mantra for subduing enemies by the Water Deity (*Varuṇa*).
The mantra is: Oṃ varuṇanāgabhūtapretaye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. When proceeding toward the west, [recite this].
First, raise this banner.
Visualize Varuṇa leading immeasurable venomous nāgas,
brandishing various weapons, charging against that host of enemies.
In the northwest, there is a blue flag;
upon the flag is painted Vāyu,
riding a deer.
The right hand holds a banner,
and the left hand rests on the hip.
The person holding the banner recites the mantra for subduing enemies through the Wind Deity (Vāyu).
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajravedhakṣarudhipāte hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. When traveling toward the western direction, [recite this].
First, raise this banner.
Visualize the Wind Deity leading immeasurable kings of the garuḍas,
brandishing various weapons to charge against that host of enemies.
In the north, one makes a yellow flag.
On the flag is painted the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa,
riding upon a ghost.
The right hand holds a jeweled stūpa,
and the left hand rests upon the hip.
The person holding the banner recites the mantra for King Vaiśravaṇa to subdue enemies.
The mantra is: Oṃ kucivara-ya-kṣa-ṭi-p-p-ta-ye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. When proceeding toward the north, [recite this].
First, raise this banner.
Visualize that the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa leads an immeasurable host of yakṣas,
brandishing various weapons, to charge against the enemy forces.
In the northeast, one should set up a flag of variegated colors,
upon which is painted the god Īśāna riding a bull.
The right hand holds a trident,
with the hand resting on the hip.
The standard-bearer recites the mantra for Ishana to descend upon enemies.
The mantra is: Oṃ īśāna-pūjita-tejo-vardhaye. When traveling in the northeast, [recite this].
First, raise this banner.
Visualize the deity Īśāna leading an immeasurable host of ghostly soldiers and generals,
brandishing various weapons, charging against that enemy force.
The Great General himself recites the mantra of Acala Vidyārāja,
visualizing his own body as becoming Acala Vidyārāja.
He further visualizes Acala Vidyārāja issuing commands to the Heavenly Kings of the eight directions, saying:
"Each of you shall lead immeasurable hosts of troops to crush those rebellious enemies.
While their great generals remain unslain,
recite the mantra of the Vidyārāja Acala."
If one performs this rite, those thieves shall surely be extinguished; of this there is no doubt.
Thereupon, he spoke the mantra of the Noble Acala Vidyārāja.
The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa*. [I] vow that the military forces of [Name], may they crush those rebellious enemies.
May that rebellious traitor suffer a great defeat.
Furthermore, recite the name of the rebel: *ṣa-pa-tsa-ya hūṃ tra-tsa haṃ kham*. If one is on a military expedition with the eight banners deployed outside, [recite this].
Each army commander and his soldiers shall encamp and take up lodging according to their respective original directions.
Likewise, each shall erect eight banners according to their respective original directions.
The banner-bearers shall burn *agallochum* incense.
One should make offerings of pure and clean food and drink.
The great general of the original direction’s banner should reside therein,
burning the most excellent and sublime aloeswood incense.
One should also make offerings of pure food and fashion a stone image of the Vidyārāja Acala,
twelve finger-widths in height, with the form of that person drawn upon it.
Furthermore, write down their names and place them upon this stone image to suppress them;
in this way, they shall naturally be extinguished before long.
Regarding the *One-Scroll Dharma for the Immovable Wisdom King to Pacify and Stabilize the State and the Family*, the *Secret Record of the Eight Families* states:

"The *One-Scroll Dharma for the Immovable Wisdom King to Pacify and Stabilize the State and the Family* was transmitted by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi to King Wu Hai, outside of the formal records."

In the first year of the Kenwa era (1841), the year of the Metal-Ox (辛酉), during the autumn moon following the Empress’s birthday, this manuscript was requested from Chikaku Kyōin in Rakudō; further copies were collated, national characters (*kokuji*) were punctuated, and the woodblocks were carved.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Kaidō of Kangi-in, Hōzan, Izumi Province.

On the twenty-seventh day of the eighth month of the autumn in the third year of the Bunsei era (1820), the year of the Wood-Dragon (庚辰), the proofreading was completed using the manuscript of Ajari Shuyō in black ink. [Seal: Ryūgan]. On the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the autumn in the fourth year of the Bunsei era (1821), the year of the Earth-Snake (辛巳), the proofreading was completed once more in red ink using the manuscript of Bikshu Sen’yū of Nisshō-ji, Banchō.
